title: Methods Research Navigator
text:
Definitions of methods research
Welcome!
This website is under construction. It will soon host the new Typology of Methods Research (TYPE-ME) - a living resource for methods researchers who work in the context of health research and psychology. The typology is based on an ongoing consensus study.
Once the typology is ready, we plan the following next steps:
You are invited to explore the current prototype:
Methodological research (MR) aims to develop, evaluate, refine, guide, or (de-)implement research methods, or synthesize existing MR.
The targets of MR are research methods across the whole research lifecycle, including the methods for planning (e.g., formulating research questions or determining sample size), conducting (e.g., recruiting participants or collecting measurements), analyzing and interpreting (e.g., statistical or qualitative analysis), reporting (e.g., reporting checklists or journal standards), summarizing (e.g., systematic reviews), evaluating (e.g., risk of bias tools or peer review), and implementing research (e.g., clinical practice guidelines or decision aids).
In addition to research methods, MR also addresses the underlying research challenges that demand methodological solutions (e.g., missing data or conflicts of interest) and the consequences of methodological choices (e.g., biases in observational studies or limitations of significance thresholds for p-values).
For this typology, we narrowed the scope to MR on research methods used in health research.

title: Methods Research Navigator
text:
The typology
We defined methodological study types along two broad dimensions: by approach (“What are the different ways in which we can answer methodological research questions?”), which includes 15 types (Table 1), and by purpose (“What are the different objectives or research questions of MR?”), which includes 13 types (Table 2). For each type, we suggest preferred and alternative terms, provide a definition, boundary notes, and show examples. Technically, the detailed typology is a faceted taxonomy with two facets corresponding to the two dimensions approach and purpose. In this manuscript, we present the two facets in separate tables while the website provides a more interactive format that allows collapsing and expanding of details.
The two dimensions are cross-cutting because one approach can serve several purposes and one purpose can draw on different approaches. For example, the approach “review of applied methods” can serve the purposes “describe current practice”, “identify the need for new methods”, or “evaluate the implementation of methods”. An example from the purpose domain is “development of methods guidance”, for which one can consider input from various approaches such as a systematic review of MR, qualitative studies involving interest-holders, or a consensus study. To make this cross-cutting structure explicit, the tables provide for each approach examples of typical purposes and for each purpose examples of typical approaches in the 3rd column
The ordering of approaches does not impose a hierarchy of strength, such as progression from “weak” to “strong” approaches. While some approaches may, in certain contexts, advance understanding in a more compelling way than another, rather than a linear journey, the typology describes a research ecosystem - a house with many interconnecting rooms of different types. The ordering of purposes broadly reflects the lifecycle of a method,(Heinze2024) beginning with assessing the status quo and research needs and ending with de-implementing methods that researchers should no longer use.

title: 1 Theory-based methods research
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels:
Methodological research that reaches its conclusions through tightly applied theory such as mathematical derivation, proof, logic, philosophy of science, or specific theoretical frameworks such as directed acyclic graphs.

title: 2 Simulation study
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: in silico study
Simulation studies experimentally apply one or more methods to a large number of simulated datasets. The datasets mimic studies and are generated under specified assumptions, usually with some element of randomness. Software then systematically applies the method(s) under investigation to each dataset to understand how they perform in general. A unique feature and strength is that one can modify the underlying truth, which allows assessing bias and the validity of precision measures under varying conditions. A limitation is that simulated scenarios may not fully capture the complexities of real studies with human error arising during data collection or methods application.

title: 3 Experimental analysis of real datasets
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels:
These studies apply methods to datasets from real studies, often drawn from published studies or repositories. Unlike simulations, the data retain real-world complexity, including variability, measurement error, or missing values and thus provide evidence on method performance in a realistic settings. The number of analyzed datasets varies from large collections that support stronger inferences to single datasets with limited generalizability.

title: 4 Reliability and agreement studies
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: Multi-researcher same-method study
These studies treat methods (such as risk of bias tools, software, or analysis plans) as instruments and involve multiple users (humans, teams, or artificial intelligences) who apply one method to the same set of cases (usually studies or datasets). Analyses assess consistency across applications: reliability studies assess how well ratings distinguish cases despite variability across raters, often using the intraclass correlation coefficient. Agreement studies assess the similarity of results across raters, often using kappa statistics or Bland–Altman plots. Reproducibility studies are a special case of agreement studies and assess whether independent teams can obtain the same results as the original study team by re-running the statistical workflow on the same data.

title: 4 Reliability and agreement studies
text:
A strength of these studies is that they quantify variability introduced by method users.
A challenge is that results depend on case difficulty and user experience, and consistency does not necessarily indicate correctness.

title: 5 Methodological randomized study
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: methodological trial; randomized methodological comparison
Randomised studies treat methods as interventions. They usually randomise individual humans (researchers, research participants or other interest holders such as peer reviewers or methods users), groups of humans (such as study teams, consensus panels, or research environments) to apply, consider, or receive training in one or more alternative methods. Possible outcomes include effect estimates, study processes such as recruitment or retention, or characteristics of study reports such as clarity, completeness, or use of appropriate methods. This type includes but is not limited to randomised studies embedded within other studies.

title: 5 Methodological randomized study
text:
A strength of randomised studies is that they allow causal conclusions about methodological interventions as humans understand and implement them under realistic conditions.
A limitation is feasibility, especially when interventions target studies or research environments rather than individual researchers or study participants.

Definition and typical features
Alternative labels:
These studies use questionnaires to collect experiences, opinions, and feedback from larger samples of researchers and other interest-holders on methodological issues. They typically use random or stratified sampling to maximise representativeness. Analyses are usually quantitative. For open-ended questions, researchers may apply qualitative analysis to classify responses before analyzing them quantitatively.

title: 8 Consensus study
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels:
These studies use formal consensus methods, such as Delphi studies or the Nominal Group Technique, and involve researchers and other interest-holders. Data collection may rely on surveys or qualitative methods. In contrast to surveys or qualitative studies that document a range of views, consensus studies seek to move participants towards a shared position. They usually employ a longitudinal design with multiple rounds of feedback, item ratings, or discussions.

title: 8 Consensus study
text:
Strengths include the structured synthesis of expert opinion and persuasiveness.
Limitations include the dependency of panel composition and process design.

title: 9 Review of applied methods
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: methodological studies;1; 2 meta-research;3 research-on-research; systematic surveys; scoping review; among many more terms that appear in practice4 with little consensus5
Reviews of applied methods examine how researchers implement methods in health research or which challenges they encounter. They sample and systematically analyze studies or other applications of methods such as in guideline panels. Sources of such applications include published journal articles, trial registries, preprints, or other sources. Sampling strategies are important and may be random to assess prevalence, purposeful to focus on high-impact studies, stratified to ensure representation of subgroups, matched such as pairs of protocols and corresponding publications, or complete. Reviews of applied methods may be nested within systematic review of health research. Typical outcomes are items of quality such as appropriate use of a method or transparent reporting. The analysis is usually based on simple quantitative measures, such as prevalence. Researchers often extract data using pre-specified forms, sometimes based on pre-existing frameworks (such as reporting guidelines) or use qualitative methods to derive categories.

title: 10 Meta-epidemiological study
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: analytical study of applied methods
Meta-epidemiological studies draw on the same sources as reviews of applied methods, but they focus on how variation in methodological practice relates to variation in study results or other outcomes, analogous to how epidemiologists examine relationships between exposures and health outcomes. Researchers typically assemble a stratified or matched sample of studies that applied either of two or more alternative methods and use meta-regression to quantify differences in the corresponding results. The analysis typically requires multi-level modelling in one or two steps.

title: 10 Meta-epidemiological study
text:
A strength is that these studies reflect real-world applications of methods, including human error.
A limitation is the high risk of confounding, which can arise at multiple levels, including differences in study populations, research questions, or measurement procedures.

title: 11 Scoping review of methods research
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels:
Scoping reviews include a broad research question and a systematic search, and aim to provide an overview of existing methods research on a methodological topic or available methods discussed in such methods research. Scoping reviews may present simple descriptive statistics (absolute and relative frequencies), often based on a qualitative categorisation or mapping against some pre-existing framework. They do not typically include a quality assessment or synthesis of study results.

title: 9 Develop guidance for understanding and applying methods
text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: methods guidance; tutorial; best practice recommendations
These studies develop guidance to help health researchers or other interest holders understand and apply methods. The guidance may include conceptual explanations, examples, recommendations for or against specific methods, or tools that operationalize guidance aids such as decision algorithms, step-by-step tutorials, templates, or code for statistical software. The development process may combine multiple approaches of methods research.

title: 9 Develop guidance for understanding and applying methods
text:
Typical approaches and corresponding examples
Approaches to develop methods guidance greatly vary and include: Theory-based methods research: Covariate adjustment in trials;1 credibility criteria for subgroup effects, some criteria based on theoretical reasoning.2
Simulation study: Guidance on using matching in cluster trials; 3 Guidance for variable screening in high dimensional survival analysis; 4 estimation of diagnostic test accuracy without reference standard.5
Experimental analysis of real datasets: Guidance for using machine learning for abstract screening; 6 Framework for prospective meta-analysis, tested in 4 real projects.7
Qualitative study involving researchers or other interest-holders in health research: Q-methodology, focus groups, content analysis, and workshops to produce guidance on creating summaries for trial participants.8
Consensus study among researchers or other interest-holders in health research: Guidance on factors to consider when inviting multiple interest-holder groups to research, based on Delphi; 9 Guidance on handling missing data in trials, based on Nominal Group Technique.10
Review of applied methods: recommendations for the use of directed acyclic graphs.11
Scoping review of methods research: A scoping review of methods papers informed guidance on integrating qualitative methods in randomized trials of complex interventions;12 A scoping review of methods papers informed guidance for developing core outcome sets.13
Qualitative synthesis of methods research: Review with qualitative synthesis of guidance for the evaluation and updating of clinical prediction models;14 review of methods research on saturation in qualitative studies;15 review of methods for confidence intervals in adaptive trials.16
Informal approaches: preventing common misunderstandings of randomisation;17 tutorial for sample size calculation in cluster trials;18 explanation why guidelines should seldom make good practice statements.19

text:
Definition and typical features
Alternative labels: risk-of-bias tools; critical appraisal tools
These studies develop scales to help health researchers or other interest holders assess methodological rigor, including risk of bias or broader trustworthiness, in a standardized way. Such scales typically use multiple signalling questions with predefined response options, sometimes combined into a summary measure. The development process may combine multiple methods research approaches.
